Kauśika
(‘a descendent of [the sage] Kuśika’)
------------------------------------------
Vedic studies and the performance of severe austerities can bestow upon a person special powers. However, the sincere and devoted performance of one’s duties in life also can confer such powers is a fact that has been stressed in our epics and mythological lore.
One of the well-known stories narrated in the Mahābhārata (Vanaparva 209) is that of a ब्राह्मण ascetic named कौशिक. Once, he was sitting for meditation under a tree. It so happened that a crane sitting on the tree eased itself and its faeces fell upon him. He opened his eyes and gazed at it with an angry look. And lo! the poor bird was reduced to ashes in no time!
Later on कौशिक went into the nearby village for alms and stood in front of a होउसे, calling the attention of the inmates. When the lady of the होउसे came out with the alms after a long time, the sage कौशिक stared at her with an angry look. She however coolly said that she was not a poor crane to be affected by his looks! Ashamed of his behaviour and astonished at her psychic insight, he asked her for guidance. After declaring that she got everything by devotedly serving her husband, she directed him to another great teacher धर्मव्याध. कौशिक went to him and was fully enlightened on the various aspects and secrets of धर्म.
Kauśika is also the name of another sage, a simpleton, who spoke the ‘truth’ about some travellers who were hiding in his hermitage, to the robbers pursuing them. These robbers killed those travellers and took away their belongings. A part of this sin accrued to कौशिक also. The lesson of this episode is that truth should bring about what is good to people. What harms them, though it may be a literal truth, is not truth in the real sense (Mahābhārata, Karṇaparva 72).
There is a dharmaśāstra attributed to one कौशिक. He has been quoted by other writers but the original is not available now.
Kauśika was also the name of विश्वामित्र because he was the grandson of कुश.

Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa
------------------------------------------
The वेदस् are generally divided into two sections: the मन्त्र and the ब्राह्मण. Sometimes, this division is extended by rearranging and adding two more sections, the Āraṇyaka and the Upaniṣad.
The Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa (2500 B. C.) (also called Śāṅkhāyana Brāhmaṇa) is one of the two ब्राह्मणस् of the Ṛgveda that is available now, the other one being Aitareya Brāhmaṇa. While some scholars feel that the Kauṣītaki and the Śāṅkhāyana ब्राह्मणस् are different, others opine that the former belongs to the शाङ्खायन-śākhā or recension and hence the same. There is a third view that शाङ्खायन was a disciple of Kauṣītaki and the author could be either of them.
There are 30 adhyāyas or chapters divided into 226 khaṇḍas or sections. Each khaṇḍa contains long passages in prose.
Like the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, this work also devotes the major part to the delineation of the details of sacrifices like अग्न्याधान, अग्निहोत्र, Darśapūrṇa-māsa, चातुर्मास्य and Somayāgas.
A few special features of this ब्राह्मण may now be given:
The tradition of gotras and pravaras had already taken root in the society.
The ṛṣis were well-versed in the science of health. They had recognised that certain diseases appear as a result of the change of seasons.
There were kings with large and disciplined armies.
People in North India were experts in Grammar.
The names of the lunar months like चैत्र and Vaiśākha are mentioned here. So also the eight names of शिव like रुद्र and पशुपति. विष्णु and शिव seem to have been equally honoured.
Immolation of animals in sacrifices and ड़्लेस्ह्-एअतिन्ग् have been condemned.
See also AITAREYA BRĀHMAṆA.

Kauśika Gṛhyasūtras
------------------------------------------
It is the same as Kauśika Sūtras. See KAUŚIKA SŪTRAS for details.

Kauṣītaki ब्राह्मण Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
Though not counted among the ten important Upaniṣads—popularly called ‘Daśopaniṣads’—the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad is nevertheless considered as a very ancient and important Upaniṣad. Two of its statements (vide 3.2; 3.8; 4.19) have been discussed in the Brahmasūtras (

-18).
Also known as Kauṣītaki or Kauṣītaka Upaniṣad, it forms chapters 3 to 6 of the 15 chapters of the Kauṣītaki Āraṇyaka which itself is attached to the Brāhmaṇa of the same name.
It is a fairly long work in four adhyāyas or chapters. Each of these contains long prose passages, the total number of such passages being 32, comprising 697 sentences.
The Upaniṣad opens with a narrative, leading to a discussion on एस्छतोलोग्य्. Citra Gāṅgyāyani, a king, invites आरुणि to be the chief priest of the sacrifice he was going to conduct. आरुणि deputes his son श्वेतकेतु for it. However, on seeing the young श्वेतकेतु, the king puts him a question about the world where he would be placed (after death) after the performance of the sacrifice. Since श्वेतकेतु did not know the answer, he goes back to his ड़थेर् to know the same.
The ड़थेर् too, is ignorant of the answer and hence comes back to the king for being instructed, along with his son. (Compare this with Chāndogya Upaniṣad

-5).
Though this is against the normal tradition (that a ब्राह्मण should become a disciple of a क्षत्त्रिय), the king accedes to his request.
Those inferior sādhakas who die here, go to the Candraloka, the world of मोओन्, the same as स्वर्ग or हेअवेन्. After exhausting their पुण्य or merit, they return to this world.
Those, on the other hand, who have performed निष्कामकर्म or desireless actions and upāsanā or meditation on God, go to ब्रह्मलोक by the देवयान path, the path of gods.
There is a highly poetic description of ब्रह्मलोक in this section.
The new entrant is received with great pomp by five hundred apsaras or nymphs. He then comes to the lake Āra, but crosses it by his मिन्द्. He later crosses the river Virajā, also with his मिन्द्, shaking off his good and evil deeds.
There are other descriptions of his coming to a divine tree called Ilya, the city Sālajja, entering the abode अपराजिता, the hall Vibhu, the throne Vicakṣaṇa, the conch Amitaujas and so on. Obviously all these symbolise his gaining greater and greater glory of ब्रह्मा.
The second chapter is concerned mainly with the प्राण, the vital breath and its upāsanā or meditation. प्राण, equated to ब्रह्मन्, is imagined as an emperor being served by the senses and the मिन्द्.
A rite called ‘Ekadhanāvarodhana’ is described to enable the वानप्रस्थ or the forest recluse to obtain wealth that is necessary for performing any sacrifice.
The internal अग्निहोत्र and some upāsanās in the form of जप of certain mantras attributed to प्रतर्दन and Sarvajit Kauṣītaki are described next.
Rites for preventing the death of children before one’s own, for the long life of sons, the superiority of the mukhya-प्राण or chief प्राण over all the sense-organs and the sampradāna-कर्म wherein the ड़थेर् on his death-bed transmits his energies to his son are the other items described here.
The third chapter starts with an ancient anecdote. प्रतर्दन, a great king, after death goes to the world of इन्द्र. He is offered a boon by इन्द्र. On प्रतर्दन requesting इन्द्र to choose an appropriate boon for himself, इन्द्र starts teaching him about mukhyaprāṇa (the chief प्राण), which he himself has attained. This mukhyaprāṇa is prajñā, intelligence or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. It itself is ब्रह्मन्.
This chapter ends with a description of the departure of the mukhyaprāṇa from the body along with all the senses.
The fourth—the last—chapter starts with a dialogue between the proud बालाकि, a descendant of the sage गर्ग, and the king अजातशत्रु. Though, at first, बालाकि starts teaching the king, he very soon discovers to his dismay that the king is far superior in the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्! The king then teaches him that it is the आत्मन्, the pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, which is pervading the whole body and which is behind all the senses. One who knows this आत्मन् becomes the sovereign, attains overlordship.
See also UPANIṢADS.

Kauṣītaki Gṛhyasūtras
------------------------------------------
The गृह्यसूत्रस् and the धर्म-sūtras are, in a way, forerunners of the later dharmaśāstra literature. The Kauṣītaki Gṛhyasūtras, belonging to the Ṛgveda is attributed to the sage Śāmbavya. Hence it is also called Śāmbavya Gṛhyasūtras.
It is in five adhyāyas or chapters, each containing a number of sūtras. The topics of उपनयन (investiture with sacred thread) and विवाह (marriage) are dealt with in great detail. Śrāddha (obsequial rites) is another subject that finds a place here.

Kauśika Sūtras
------------------------------------------
The Atharvaveda (also spelt as the Atharvaṇaveda) is the last of the four वेदस्. Chronologically speaking, it is perhaps a later composition. That is why, not only is its language more sophisticated and philosophical ideas more clear, it also includes many subjects of social importance, more fully developed.
Five Sūtra works are attached to this Veda as detailed appendices, expounding the rites and concepts in greater detail. They are: Kauśika Sūtras, Vaitāna Sūtras, Nakṣatrakalpa Sūtras, Āṅgirasakalpa Sūtras and Śāntikalpa Sūtras.
The Kauśika Sūtras—sometimes titled as Kauśika Gṛhyasūtras also—is an independent work attributed to the sage कौशिक about whom nothing is known. Though the Vedic scholars generally agree that this is the oldest of the five works mentioned, no possible date has been assigned to it.
It has 14 adhyāyas or chapters. Each adhyāya has several kaṇḍikās or sections, the kaṇḍikās, again, comprising several individual sūtras. There are 3008 sūtras distributed among 141 kaṇḍikās.
A commentary called Kauśikabhāṣya by Dārila (or Hārila) and a Paddhati (gloss) by one Keśava, son of Someśvara, are available. The former work is incomplete and ends at the 48th kaṇḍikā, the rest being, perhaps, lost for ever.
Bhaṭṭāribhaṭṭa and वासुदेव are two other commentators mentioned by some scholars.
The contents of the sūtras embrace a variety of subjects ranging from वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् right up to medical science and black magic.
A very brief summary of subjects may now be attempted here:
Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices; various rites for getting wisdom, securing desires, harmony, power, aversion of misfortunes and so on; different kinds of charms and amulets for securing property, cattle and safety of long journeys; remedial charms for curing diseases; rites and rituals connected with women and progeny; protection against the vagaries of nature, to get rains and crops; countering the effect of witchcraft; चोरोनतिओन् of a king; Vedic studies; morning and evening oblations; prāyaścittas or expiatory rites; सṁस्कारस् like उपनयन, विवाह (marriage) and ड़ुनेरल् रितेस्; various omens and portents.
See also ATHARVAVEDA.

Kaustubha
(‘that which pervades [the universe]’)
------------------------------------------
According to the various systems of Hindu philosophy and the mystical traditions, God is both nirākāra (without any particular form) and nirguṇa (without attributes) as also sākāra and saguṇa (with form and attributes).
One of the most widely known (even from the Vedic period) and worshipped forms of God is that of विष्णु-नारायण.
Detailed descriptions of विष्णु-Nārā-yaṇa as found in the Hindu epics and the पुराणस् state that he wears an extra-ordinarily brilliant and beautiful gem called “Kaustubha” on his chest, covering the Śrīvatsa mark there.
This gem is said to have emerged out of the क्षीरसमुद्र or the ocean of milk at the time of its churning. (See SAMUDRAMATHANA for details.) It got lodged on विष्णु’s chest by itself (Mahābhārata, Ādiparva 18).
Literally, the word ‘Kaustubha’ means ‘that which pervades the whole universe’. Symbolically, it stands for all that enjoys (bhoktā), the Śrīvatsa mark representing all that is enjoyed (bhogya). The two together represent the created universe in all its aspects which itself is like an ornament for God.

Kausalyā
------------------------------------------
She was the daughter of a king Bhānumān, the eldest queen of दशरथ and the मोथेर् of श्रीराम.
Daśaratha and कौसल्या were कश्यप and अदिति reborn.
See RĀMĀYAṆA for details.
